rationale: Psalm 77 remembers the sea crossing: "The waters saw You, O God" (77:16), "Your path led through the sea, Your way through the mighty waters, but Your footprints were not to be found" (77:19), and "You led Your people like a flock by the hand of Moses and Aaron" (77:20, BSB). The psalm shares a theme with Matthew 14:25-26, God making His own way in the sea, but not the wording. Its Septuagint line (en tē thalassē hē hodos sou, "in the sea is Your way") has no verb for walking, and as Andrew Perriman reports Richard Hays pointing out, the psalm speaks of a path through the sea, not a walk on it. The same theme recurs in Isaiah 43:16 ("who makes a way in the sea") and 51:10 ("who made a road in the depths of the sea", BSB). So the type is motif, not allusion. The label is plausible because named readers propose this background. Perriman leans toward an exodus background for Mark's version, citing Psalm 77:19-20 and reporting Morna Hooker's view that Jesus' intention to pass by acts out Israel's passing through the sea. Alexander MacLaren, preaching on Matthew's scene, says Christ's "paths are in the great waters," close to the King James wording of 77:19 ("thy path in the great waters"), without naming the psalm. Perriman's argument concerns Mark; no source read here argues the link for Matthew specifically.
